sections.label: Content note
sections.body: **Content note:** this page discusses abuse, neglect, restraint and the deaths of people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. [Where to report abuse is listed below.](#kop-ri-report)

sections.label: Not the troubled teen industry
sections.heading: Not the troubled teen industry
sections.body:
Group homes and other residential services for adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) are not part of the troubled teen industry, and Kids Over Profits does not track them. The people who live in them are adults, with a rights movement of their own led by self-advocates.

What ties the two together is people held in facilities run for profit. Disabled adults live in homes run by providers the state pays to house them, and some of the same companies and private equity owners run youth programs too. Restraint, seclusion and drugs given to control behavior are documented in both, and disabled young people in youth programs age into adult services, sometimes with the same company.

We are not the experts on this system. The self-advocates and organizations listed below are.

sections.label: What the industry is
sections.heading: What this system is
sections.body:
Most adults with IDD who get paid support live with family. Of about 1.38 million people served by state developmental disability agencies on June 30, 2021, the newest national count, 63 percent lived in a relative's home. About 299,000 lived in a group home, another group setting or an intermediate care facility.[^1]

Medicaid pays for nearly all of it. In fiscal year 2021, Medicaid home and community-based services (HCBS) waivers paid $47.1 billion for 953,571 people with IDD, and Intermediate Care Facilities for Individuals with Intellectual Disabilities (ICF/IIDs), a Medicaid benefit with its own federal rules, cost $8.68 billion for 63,085 people.[^1]

The large state institutions are not all gone. In 2021, 106 state-run facilities for 16 or more people held an average of 15,049 residents a day, down from 194,650 in 1967; 18 states and the District of Columbia had closed all of theirs.[^1]

Private providers run almost everything else: of about 232,000 places where people with IDD lived outside a family home in 2021, states ran 1,940.[^1] Those providers were long mostly regional nonprofits and church groups. Private equity firms made more than 1,000 acquisitions of disability and elder care providers from 2013 to 2023,[^2] and own two of the largest operators:

- **Sevita**, formerly The MENTOR Network and Civitas Solutions, says it has 60,000 employees serving 70,000 people.[^3] Private equity has owned it since Madison Dearborn Partners bought it in 2001. Vestar Capital Partners followed in 2006 and took it public as Civitas Solutions in 2014 ([corporatization timeline](/corporatization/)), and Centerbridge Partners and The Vistria Group bought it in March 2019.[^4]
- **BrightSpring Health Services**, formerly ResCare, owned more than 600 residential facilities when the private equity firm KKR took control in March 2019.[^5] It filed to go public in January 2024.[^6]

sections.label: History
sections.heading: Where these homes came from
sections.body:
Group homes for adults with IDD grew out of the institutions built in the 1800s to hold children labelled "idiotic" and "feebleminded." Those institutions are also among the roots of the troubled teen industry ([developmental disabilities and eugenics](/idd-timeline/)).

The first opened on Randall's Island in New York in 1847 and in Massachusetts in 1848, at the school later called the Fernald Center, whose administrators included eugenicists who called for disabled children to be kept apart. Indiana passed the first forced sterilization law in 1907; California sterilized more than 20,000 people, many of them adolescents in state care. In *Buck v. Bell* (1927) the Supreme Court upheld the sterilization of Carrie Buck, a teenager held at the Virginia Colony for Epileptics and Feeble-Minded. From 1914 the juvenile courts explained delinquency as "mental defect" too ([juvenile justice timeline](/juvenile-justice-timeline/)).

Private schools followed. Helena Devereux opened hers in Pennsylvania in 1912; by 1983 Devereux was a national chain housing young people with IDD on Medicaid and public school money ([corporatization timeline](/corporatization/)). The Menninger Clinic's Southard School, opened in 1926 for children with intellectual disabilities, became a prototype for the psychoanalytic residential treatment center ([the birth of the TTI](/birth-of-the-tti/)).

Deinstitutionalization began in the 1960s, but underfunding left gaps that private facilities filled, and from 1965 Medicaid let public money follow a child into a private placement ([the birth of the TTI](/birth-of-the-tti/)). Behavior modification moved between the two systems. In 1965 Ivar Lovaas published his use of electric shock on autistic children at UCLA. Applied Behavior Analysis, defined in 1968, was first used to enforce compliance in disabled and autistic children, and in 1971 Matthew Israel founded the Behavior Research Institute, now the Judge Rotenberg Center ([experimental group psychology](/experimental-group-psychology/)). Point systems, levels and punishment for "noncompliance" passed back and forth between these programs and the ones built for troubled teens.

sections.label: How it is connected to the TTI
sections.heading: How it is connected to the troubled teen industry
sections.body:
### The same companies

- **Sevita / The MENTOR Network** serves adults and children with IDD and children in foster care.[^3] The Senate Finance Committee made it the case study of its 2017 investigation of for-profit foster care,[^7] which raised concerns about treatment and deaths among foster children in its care.[^8] Its brand NeuroRestorative runs [14 group homes for young people in Illinois](/facility/neurorestorative-il/) that are in our records. In 2024 Florida moved to revoke NeuroRestorative's Florida license over its use of restraint and seclusion on children.[^9]
- **ResCare / BrightSpring** called itself the nation's largest private provider of services for people with developmental disabilities in 2011. The same annual report describes residential treatment for young people with emotional and behavioral issues and for juveniles in the justice system, foster care, and 14 Job Corps centers for youth ages 16 to 24.[^10] BrightSpring still runs foster care and youth services.[^11] Two West Virginia youth programs under the ResCare name are in our records.
- **Devereux Advanced Behavioral Health**, a nonprofit, runs youth residential programs, [43 of them in our records](/operator/devereux-advanced-behavioral-health/), and treats children with IDD in 12 specialized programs.[^12] It also runs more than 60 adult group homes in New Jersey alone, for nearly 300 adults,[^13] and adult IDD homes in Massachusetts.[^14]
- **The Judge Rotenberg Educational Center** in Canton, Massachusetts, serves children and adults[^15] and is the only facility in the country known to use electric skin shock on the people in its care. The FDA estimated that about 50 people had treatment plans that included it.[^16] The FDA banned the devices in 2020; a federal appeals court vacated the ban in July 2021, Congress gave the FDA clear authority in 2022, and the FDA proposed a new ban in March 2024.[^17] As of October 2026 no final rule had been published. [The center is in our records](/facility/judge-rotenberg-educational-center-ma/).
- **AdvoServ**, which served children and adults with severe intellectual and developmental disabilities, was bought by the private equity firm Wellspring Capital Management in 2015.[^18] After ProPublica reported the deaths of three teenagers in its care and its frequent use of restraints, it renamed itself Bellwether Behavioral Health in 2017.[^19] In 2019 New Jersey moved its 62 adult group homes to other providers.[^20] Its youth program in Delaware is in our records ([corporatization timeline](/corporatization/)).

### The same practices

In 1999 the GAO linked 24 deaths in one year to restraint or seclusion in facilities for people with mental illness or what was then called mental retardation. Federal rules then covered restraint in ICFs and nursing homes, but not in psychiatric hospitals, children's residential centers or community group homes.[^21] Federal ICF/IID rules now allow drugs to control behavior only as part of a plan to end the behavior, with team approval and a yearly attempt to withdraw them.[^22] Across many states in 2024-25, 37 percent of adults with IDD in group settings took medication for "behavioral challenges," and only 55 percent of them had a behavior plan.[^23]

### From one system to the other

Disabled children are placed in youth programs, sometimes for most of their childhood: the Senate Finance Committee found Devereux stays of up to 6,928 days, almost 19 years, on its Florida campus. A 19-year-old autistic resident died after a restraint at Laurel Heights, a Universal Health Services youth hospital in Georgia.[^12] Several of the companies above run services on both sides of the age line.

sections.label: What investigations found
sections.heading: What investigations have found
sections.body:
- **KKR and BrightSpring (BuzzFeed News, 2022).** In seven states, KKR owned 16 percent of the intermediate care facilities and received 40 percent of the most serious citations, more than 500, from March 2019 to the end of 2021. The company took out $1.1 billion in new loans and paid more than $135 million a year in interest. KKR and BrightSpring disputed the findings.[^5]
- **The MENTOR Network (Senate Finance Committee, 2020).** REM Iowa had recurring critical incidents, including failures to report abuse or neglect,[^24] and MENTOR Oregon showed "a consistent pattern of substandard care."[^25][^26]
- **Unreported injuries (HHS, 2016 to 2018).** Inspector General audits found that group homes did not report 99 percent of critical incidents to investigators in Connecticut, 95 percent in Maine and 58 percent in Massachusetts, where one resident suffered head lacerations while aides restrained them.[^27] A 2018 joint report by the Inspector General, the Administration for Community Living and the Office for Civil Rights found media reports of health and safety problems in group homes in 49 states.[^28]
- **Illinois (Chicago Tribune, 2016).** "Suffering in Secret" found more than 1,300 cases of documented harm in group homes and their day programs since July 2011, and at least 42 deaths linked to abuse or neglect, far more than the state had reported.[^29]
- **New York (The New York Times, 2011).** "Abused and Used" found that the state kept workers who had physically or sexually abused residents and rarely reported abuse allegations to law enforcement.[^30] The state then changed how workers accused of abuse are disciplined.[^31]

sections.label: Where to report abuse
sections.heading: Where to report abuse
sections.body:
- **If someone is in danger now**, call 911.
- **Adult Protective Services** takes reports of abuse, neglect and exploitation of adults with disabilities in most states. In some states a separate agency handles adults with developmental disabilities, or adults under 60. The National Adult Protective Services Association keeps [the reporting contact for every state and territory](https://www.napsa-now.org/help-in-your-area/).
- **The Eldercare Locator**, run by the federal government, refers callers to local agencies, mainly for older adults: call or text 1-800-677-1116, or visit [eldercare.acl.gov](https://eldercare.acl.gov/).
- **Protection and Advocacy agencies** are independent disability rights agencies in every state and territory. Find yours in the [National Disability Rights Network directory](https://www.ndrn.org/about/ndrn-member-agencies/).
- **Medicaid Fraud Control Units** investigate abuse and neglect of residents of health care facilities and board and care facilities, and of Medicaid enrollees in other settings ([HHS Office of Inspector General](https://oig.hhs.gov/fraud/medicaid-fraud-control-units-mfcu/)).
- Also tell the state agency that licenses the home or pays for the services.
- **988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline**, 24 hours: call or text [988](tel:988).

Our [reporting directory](/report-abuse/) lists agencies state by state.

sections.label: Organizations to learn from
sections.heading: Learn from the people who work on this
sections.body:
- [Self Advocates Becoming Empowered (SABE)](https://www.sabeusa.org/): The nationwide organization of self-advocates, people with intellectual and developmental disabilities speaking for themselves. Its priorities include closing institutions.
- [Autistic Self Advocacy Network (ASAN)](https://autisticadvocacy.org/about-asan/): A national disability rights organization run by and for autistic people.
- [ADAPT](https://adapt.org/): A grassroots disability rights group known for direct action for the right to live at home, not in nursing homes and institutions.
- [National Disability Rights Network (NDRN)](https://www.ndrn.org/about/): The membership organization for the Protection and Advocacy agencies and Client Assistance Programs in every state and territory.
- [The Arc of the United States](https://thearc.org/about-us/): Has advocated for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities and their families since 1950, with chapters across the country.
- [National Council on Independent Living (NCIL)](https://www.ncil.org/about/): A cross-disability organization advocating for independent living and disability rights since 1982.

sections.label: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.heading: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.body: If you live or work in this system, or you are a self-advocate or a family member, and something on this page is wrong, please [tell us](/contact/). We will correct it.
